title: Chapter 118 — Training Systems and Team Development
intro: The huddle, the drill culture, curriculum deployment, and building the bench.

sections.title: The Daily Huddle
sections.content:
Five to ten minutes before the floor opens. Everyone together. Quick wins from yesterday. Focus for today. One product highlight. One skill reminder.

The huddle is not a meeting. It is a ritual. It sets the energy for the day and keeps the team connected to the process. Stores that huddle consistently outperform stores that do not — because they start every day with shared focus.

sections.title: The Drill Culture
sections.content:
Athletes drill. Musicians drill. Surgeons drill. Salespeople should drill.

Role-playing a customer interaction is awkward. It is also the fastest way to improve. Practice the greeting. Practice discovery questions. Practice objection handling. Practice the close.

The salesperson who practiced ACRA ten times in role play handles the live objection without thinking. The one who never practiced stumbles and loses the sale.

sections.title: Building the Bench
sections.content:
Great leaders are always developing the next leader. Who on your team could step into a management role? Who has the drive, the skills, and the mindset?

Invest in those people. Give them coaching opportunities. Let them lead huddles. Put them in situations that stretch their skills.

If you are the only person who can run the team, you have built a dependency, not a team.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating training systems, ask:

Is there a daily huddle — or does the day start without direction?
Does the team practice skills through drills and role play?
Is the manager developing future leaders — or hoarding responsibility?
Is training consistent — or sporadic and reactive?
